item.title: Bit Flip
item.description:
What you just did

Computers store every number as a row of on/off switches called bits. Each switch is worth double the one to its right: 1, 2, 4, 8, and so on up to 128. Eight of them together make a byte, which can hold any whole number from 0 to 255. The row of 0s and 1s under the number is that byte, written the way a computer stores it. So when you made 37, you wrote 00100101, which is 37 in binary.

item.title: Campus Route
item.description:
How a map app finds the fastest route

The shortest-looking route is often not the fastest one, which is why map apps don’t just pick the path with the fewest turns. They use a method worked out by the computer scientist Edsger Dijkstra in 1956 and published in 1959.

It works like this: start where you are, at 0 minutes. Then, again and again, take the closest place whose time isn’t final yet, mark its time as final, and see whether going through it gives any of its neighbors a faster time. When the destination’s time becomes final, it is guaranteed to be the fastest possible. Press Watch a computer solve it after a puzzle to see each step on the map.

item.title: Code Word
item.description:
How the clues work

Every guess must be a real word with the same number of letters as the answer. After each guess, every letter gets a mark: a filled dot means the letter is in the right spot, a ring means the word has that letter somewhere else, and a dash means it doesn’t (or not that many times). The letter buttons keep track of what you have learned.

About the words

Each day’s word is a computing term that comes up in everyday life, from the cloud to cookies to chatbots. When the puzzle ends, you’ll see a short, plain explanation of what it means.

item.title: Logic Lights
item.description:
What the gates do

Every decision a computer makes is built from tiny circuits like this one. Each gate takes signals that are on or off and passes on a new one: AND is on only when both of its inputs are on, OR is on when at least one is, NOT flips its input, and XOR (from Friday on) is on when exactly one input is on. A computer’s processor is built from gates like these, made of billions of tiny electronic switches called transistors.

Why “Watch a computer solve it” matters

A computer can simply try every combination of switches: with 6 switches there are only 64. But each extra switch doubles the count, so with 30 switches there would be over a billion combinations. Telling which circuits can ever be switched on is a famous hard problem in computer science, and much of the field is about finding cleverer ways than trying everything.

item.title: Crack the Cipher
item.description:
How the code works

Each day’s quotation is written in a substitution cipher: every letter is swapped for another letter, and the same letter is always swapped the same way. Spaces and punctuation stay put. If Q stands for E once, it stands for E everywhere.

How to crack it

Start with what you know about English. Short words help: a one-letter word is almost always A or I, and three-letter words are often THE or AND. Letter counts help even more: E, T, A, O, I and N are the most common letters in English, so the most common letters in the puzzle are good first guesses. Counting letters to break a code is called frequency analysis, and the Arab scholar al-Kindi described it in the 9th century.

Every quotation comes from a book in the public domain and was checked word for word against the book’s text at Project Gutenberg.
